title: The Three Eternal Works at the Consummation
arc: The teaching enumerates three permanent works that will be fashioned in the Light at the end of the drama — the new shining land, the binding of darkness's fire, and the sealing of sinners in the final clod — and shows how each is fixed forever by an unbreakable boundary between Light and Darkness.
reading:
This chapter describes the final, settled state of the cosmos after the spiritual war is finished. It names three works that will be fashioned in the Light, and the controlling claim about all three is that they have no beginning other than the Light itself and no end — they cannot cease willing to be. This is the doctrine that the eternal states established at the consummation are permanent: once love and wisdom have done their separating work, the resulting order is fixed, because nothing in it any longer wills its own dissolution. Good wills to remain good, and evil, now bound, can no longer break out toward anything else.

The first work is the new land which sheds light. Read correspondentially, this is the regenerated natural — the Land of Light established as the dwelling of the redeemed, the natural mind made luminous because divine truth now shines in it without obstruction. It is "appointed and turned upon this land," meaning the new order is set down precisely upon the same plane where the mingling once was: the very ground of natural existence, formerly the field of the Old Man's body and of the alien body that pressed upon the soul, is now the shining country of the New Man. Where light was once captive, light now is the ground itself.

The second work, though damaged, clearly concerns the fire of darkness, the beam of the Enemy. In the lexicon, common fire is the burning of self-love, and "the beam of the Enemy" is the projecting power of the King of Darkness. The second eternal work is therefore the permanent binding or extinguishing of self-love's active power — the fire that once threw its beam upward against the Greatness is at last quenched as a working force in the cosmos. It still exists, but it can no longer radiate; its outward operation is over.

The third work is the most fully preserved and gives the chapter its weight. It is the desolation of all the sinners — those who set themselves in their own works, who divided themselves one from another according to their bitter works. These are the souls confirmed in self-love, whose works have hardened into their identity. Their fate is described in three precise images. They shall be crucified upon the Enemy who exalted himself against the Greatness: that is, those who joined the proprium are fastened to the proprium permanently, sharing its fixed posture of opposition. They shall sojourn in the last bolos — the final compacted clod of unredeemed darkness — and into that clod shall be poured likenesses with icons of every form, meaning every shape of falsity and corrupt affection is gathered there and they are bound together with those creatures in the last bond forever. The bolos thus becomes a totalized state: an ember-pit, gloom, a shadow without number, the prison of the Enemy. Every kind of evil affection ("those creatures") is sealed inside one final state of spiritual death, and the sinners are bound with them.

The closing image is the cosmic boundary. The bolos is set with a great guard as a wall of demarcation between the two — between the Light and the Enemy — so that they may no longer strike one another nor even hear one another's voice; they shall be at great distance, separated from one another, forever and ever. This is the fixed firmament of the consummated state. In the present cosmos, light and darkness are mingled and constantly clash; in the final state, the separating work of regeneration is total: no contact, no influx across the line, no disturbance of the heavens by hell. The great guard corresponds to the divine restraining power made eternal — the Holder no longer holding back an active enemy, but holding shut a sealed prison.

Read as a single arc, the teaching is a vision of the three permanent outcomes of the whole spiritual drama: a luminous natural, a quenched fire of self-love, and a sealed clod of unredeemed evil walled off forever from the Light. Their permanence is grounded not in arbitrary decree but in the nature of will itself — each side has become wholly what it is, and neither any longer wills to be otherwise. That is why these works have no beginning except the Light from which they originate, and no end at which they could cease willing to be.
